subtitle: Binary addition, the half and full adder, the ripple-carry chain, and the same circuit made to subtract. Every figure is a live logic circuit; every truth table is generated by simulating it.

intro.body:
Let’s start with a question you can answer before reading any further: what is the one thing a computer does more than anything else? It adds. If you can build an adder, you have built the beating heart of a processor, and in this lesson you will build one from nothing but simple gates. A processor adds more often than it does anything else. Every loop counter, every array index, every multiply built from shifts and adds, every address the memory bus ever sees — all of it is addition. And the machine doing it has no concept of a number: it has wires that are either near the supply rail or near ground, and gates that combine them.

These notes build the adder up from that floor. First the four one-bit sums, then the half adder that produces them, then the full adder that can be chained, then a four-bit adder that carries a result from one stage to the next — and finally the same circuit made to subtract, and to drive a digit onto a display.

How to read these notesEvery circuit here is live. Each one carries its own Simulate button: press it and the logic solver runs that circuit, the output indicators show 0 or 1, and the sliders beneath change the inputs while it runs. A truth table under a figure is not typed out — it is produced by simulating that exact circuit for every input combination.
What this simulator does not model. Its logic pass settles instantly: it finds the stable value of every wire and stops. Real gates take time, and §9 is entirely about that time — but the figures there cannot show it, and the notes say so where it matters rather than pretending otherwise.
keynotes: A processor adds more often than it does anything else: loop counters, array indices, multiplies built from shifts and adds, and every memory address.
The adder is built up from one-bit sums to the half adder, the full adder, a four-bit ripple-carry chain, then subtraction and a display.
Every circuit is live: press Simulate, and the truth tables are produced by simulating the exact circuit.

binary-sums.body:
Here is the whole problem of addition in four lines, and you could do it in your sleep. Still, look closely, because one of the four lines hides a surprise. Binary addition has exactly four cases, and three of them are trivial. 0 + 0 is 0. 0 + 1 and 1 + 0 are both 1. The fourth case is where the hardware comes from: 1 + 1 is two, and two is not a digit in binary. It is written 10 — a 0 in this column and a 1 carried into the next.

So a one-bit adder cannot have one output. It needs two: the sum bit that stays in this column, and the carry bit that moves left. Everything else in this lesson follows from that single fact.
keynotes: Binary addition has four cases: 0 + 0 is 0, 0 + 1 and 1 + 0 are 1, and 1 + 1 is two, written 10.
A one-bit adder therefore needs two outputs: the sum bit that stays in this column and the carry bit that moves left.
The Sum column reads 0, 1, 1, 0 and the Carry column reads 0, 0, 0, 1.
binary-sums.after: Four rows is the entire specification of a one-bit adder. The rest of this lesson is that specification implemented, chained, and then bent into doing subtraction.

half-adder.body:
Now you get to build something real. Ask yourself: which two gates would give you exactly the sum and the carry from the last section? You may be surprised how simple the answer is. Wire an XOR gate and an AND gate across the same two inputs and you have a half adder: the XOR produces the sum bit, the AND produces the carry. Two gates, two inputs, two outputs, and it implements Figure 2.1 completely.

The truth table under the circuit is not typed into these notes. It is generated by driving that exact circuit through all four input combinations and reading what comes out, so if the wiring were wrong the table would be wrong in the same way — which is the only kind of table worth printing beside a circuit.
keynotes: An XOR gate and an AND gate across the same two inputs make a half adder: the XOR gives the sum and the AND gives the carry.
With both inputs high the sum output is low and the carry output is high.
It is called half because it has no carry input; it is right only for the least significant column.
half-adder.after:
Now try to use it. Adding two four-bit numbers means four columns, and every column but the rightmost has three bits arriving: the two input bits and the carry out of the column to its right. A half adder has two inputs. There is nowhere to put the carry.

That is what the name means. It is half of what a column of a real addition needs — and it is exactly right for the one column that has no carry coming in, the least significant.

ha-algebra.body: Before you go on, let’s see where the gates came from in the first place; you should know how to derive them yourself. Figure 3.1 was presented as a finished circuit, which is the wrong way round: the table comes first and the gates are derived from it. Doing that derivation properly is the skill the rest of combinational design rests on.
keynotes: A truth table with two outputs is two independent problems: the sum column and the carry column each get their own expression.
Carry is 1 in exactly one row, so C = A·B; sum is 1 in two rows, S = Ā B + A B̄, which is exclusive-OR.
Recognising XOR in a sum of products turns four gates and two inverters into one.

full-adder.body:
The half adder had a weakness that you probably spotted: it cannot accept a carry from the column beside it. Let’s fix that, and watch how little has to change. A column in the middle of an addition receives three bits: A, B and the carry out of the column to its right. Their total runs from 0 to 3, which still fits in two output bits — a sum and a carry — so the shape of the circuit does not change. Only the input count does.

A circuit that adds three bits and produces a two-bit result is a full adder, and it is the unit every wider adder is built from. Three inputs means eight rows, and the table below is again generated by running the circuit rather than by asserting it.
keynotes: A column in the middle of an addition receives three bits, A, B and the carry in, whose total runs from 0 to 3 and still fits in two output bits.
The sum is S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, 1 when an odd number of inputs is 1.
The carry out is Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B); with all three inputs at 1 both sum and carry out read 1.

fa-from-ha.body:
Here is a lovely piece of engineering thrift: you do not need to design the full adder from scratch, because you have already built its parts. The factored carry expression, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), says something structural: everything a full adder needs is already produced by two half adders. The first adds A and B. The second adds that partial sum to the carry in. Each one hands over its own carry, and the two carries are ORed together.

The OR is safe because the two carries can never both be 1. If the first half adder carried, its sum bit was 0, so the second half adder had 0 + Cin and cannot carry. Only one of the two can fire in any row, which is why an OR — rather than a second adder — finishes the job.
keynotes: A full adder is two half adders plus an OR gate: the first adds A and B, the second adds that partial sum to the carry in.
The two carries are ORed because they can never both be 1.
It behaves identically to the eight-row full adder because it computes the same two expressions.
fa-from-ha.after: Which one does hardware actually use? Neither shape is sacred. A standard-cell library implements the full adder as one optimised cell, chosen for its carry delay rather than its tidiness on paper, because the carry path is what sets the speed of everything built from it — which is §9.

ripple.body:
Now comes the satisfying bit, where you line up the little adders like people passing a bucket down a line, each one handing its carry to the next. You will see how a tiny rule, repeated, adds numbers of any length. Chaining is now mechanical. One full adder per bit; each one's carry output becomes the next one's carry input; the rightmost carry input is 0, because nothing is carried into the least significant column. The carry out of the leftmost stage is the ninth bit of an eight-bit answer — or, for our four-bit adder, the fifth bit of a five-bit answer.

The circuit below adds A = 1011 (eleven) and B = 0110 (six). Seventeen does not fit in four bits, so the sum outputs read 0001 and the carry out reads 1: together, 10001, which is seventeen.

Set your own numbersPress Simulate, then use the eight sliders. A3 is the most significant bit of A and A0 the least; the same for B. Watch which output bits change when you flip A0 — a carry from the bottom can alter every bit above it.
keynotes: A ripple-carry adder uses one full adder per bit, each carry out feeding the next carry in, and the rightmost carry in is 0.
1011 (eleven) + 0110 (six) gives sum outputs 0001 and carry out 1, together 10001, which is seventeen.
A carry from the bottom can alter every bit above it.

worked-add.body:
Let’s slow down and do the arithmetic by hand, the way you would on paper, and then check our work against the circuit. Add the two four-bit numbers of Figure 7.1 by hand, column by column, then check every bit against the circuit.

Each step is revealed one at a time. Work the column yourself before opening the next.
keynotes: Add the two four-bit numbers of Figure 7.1 by hand, column by column, then check every bit against the circuit.
Work each column yourself before opening the next step.
The carry chain is where to look first if your answer and the circuit disagree.

delay.body:
Here is a question that separates a student from an engineer: how fast is your adder? You might guess it depends on how many gates there are, but you would be wrong. Every gate takes time. Its output does not change at the instant its input does; it changes one propagation delay later, once the transistors inside have charged the next stage's input capacitance. Call that delay Δ and assume for now that every gate has the same one — a crude model, but the right one for comparing structures.

The sum outputs of a ripple-carry adder are not the problem. The carry is. It enters stage 0, leaves it, enters stage 1, and so on: the stages cannot work in parallel, because each one's answer depends on the one below it. The adder is not finished when its slowest gate is finished — it is finished when the carry has crossed every stage.
keynotes: Every gate has a propagation delay Δ, and the adder is finished when the carry has crossed every stage, not when the slowest gate finishes.
The carry from stage 0 appears after 3Δ and each later stage adds 2Δ, so the total is (2n + 1)Δ.
Ripple-carry delay is linear in the width, which is why wide fast adders are built differently.

overflow.body:
Be careful with the carry out, because it can tell you a comforting lie if you let it. You will meet a case where no carry leaves the adder and the answer is still wrong, and you should learn to spot it before it bites you in a real program. The carry out of the top stage answers one question: did the unsigned result need a fifth bit? For unsigned numbers that is the whole story — carry out 1 means the answer was too big for the width, and the value on the sum pins is the true answer modulo 16.

For signed numbers it is the wrong question. In two's complement the top bit is the sign, so a four-bit register holds −8 to +7, and the interesting failure is a result that leaves that range. Add 0111 (seven) and 0001 (one): the sum pins read 1000 and the carry out is 0. No carry left the adder, and the answer is still wrong — 1000 read as signed is −8.

The detector for signed overflow is different: overflow is the carry into the top stage disagreeing with the carry out of it, V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1. Equivalently, and more memorably: adding two numbers of the same sign and getting the opposite sign is always overflow, and adding opposite signs can never overflow.
keynotes: The carry out of the top stage answers one question: did the unsigned result need a fifth bit?
For signed numbers 0111 + 0001 gives sum pins 1000 and carry out 0, yet the answer is wrong, since 1000 is −8.
Signed overflow is V = Cn ⊕ C(n−1): same-sign operands giving the opposite sign, and opposite signs can never overflow.

subtractor.body:
What if you could subtract without building a single new circuit? You can, and the trick is lovely: the very adder you already have will do the job, with one small change that you can make in a moment. In two's complement, negating a number means inverting every bit and adding one. So A − B is A + (NOT B) + 1 — and an adder can do all of it, provided something can invert B on demand and something can supply the +1.

Both jobs are already available. An XOR gate with one input tied to a control line is a controlled inverter: with the control at 0 it passes its data input through unchanged, with the control at 1 it inverts it. And the +1 goes into the carry in of stage 0, the pin that was tied to 0 for plain addition.

One control line, called SUB, therefore turns a four-bit adder into a four-bit adder-subtractor: it feeds all four XOR gates and the carry in at once.
keynotes: In two's complement A − B is A + (NOT B) + 1, so an adder can subtract if B can be inverted on demand and +1 supplied.
An XOR gate with a control line is a controlled inverter, and the +1 goes into the carry in of stage 0.
One SUB line turns a four-bit adder into an adder-subtractor, and the carry out in subtract mode means no borrow was needed.
subtractor.after: Reading the carry out in subtract mode. It inverts its usual meaning: 1 means A ≥ B and the result is a plain positive number, while 0 means a borrow — the true answer is negative and the pins hold its two's-complement form. This is why processors distinguish 'carry' from 'borrow' in their documentation while using one physical flag for both.

display.body:
A string of 0s and 1s is no use to most people, so let’s make the answer visible to you. You will take the adder’s four sum bits and turn them into a digit you can read at a glance, just like on a pocket calculator. Four sum bits are an answer only to someone who reads binary. A BCD-to-seven-segment driver turns a four-bit value into the seven segment signals that spell that digit, and a seven-segment display lights them.

The circuit below is the adder of §7 with its sum bits taken to a driver instead of stopping at the output pins: three plus four, and the display shows a 7. Nothing about the adder changed — the bits it produced were always a number; this is just the first figure that says so in a font.

Only one digit. A single display shows 0 to 9, and a four-bit adder can reach 15. Feed it 1010 or above and the driver has no digit to show — real designs convert the binary result to BCD first, with a converter that is itself built from adders.
keynotes: A BCD-to-seven-segment driver turns a four-bit value into the seven segment signals that spell that digit.
The adder's sum bits taken to a driver show three plus four as a 7.
A single display shows 0 to 9, but a four-bit adder can reach 15.

problems.body: Now it is your turn. This is where you find out what you have really understood, and where the lesson becomes yours. Six problems over the whole lesson. Work each on paper before opening its answer; where the answer can be settled by a circuit, it carries one you can run.
keynotes: There are six problems over the whole lesson.
Work each on paper before opening its answer.

summary.body:
Look back at how far you have come: from a single bit to a circuit that adds and subtracts, and a way of reasoning about how fast it runs. You have earned the summary below, so read it slowly. Every circuit in this lesson was simulated, not asserted: the truth tables were generated by running the gates, and every figure's outputs were read off the solver. Six statements carry the rest.

  1. 1 + 1 = 10. A one-bit addition needs two outputs, a sum and a carry, and that is why adders exist at all.
  2. The half adder is S = A ⊕ B, C = A · B — complete for the least significant column, useless for any other, because it has no carry input.
  3. The full adder is S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), and it is exactly two half adders with their carries ORed.
  4. Ripple-carry chains them, one per bit, and costs (2n + 1) gate delays — linear in the width, which is why wide fast adders are built differently.
  5. The carry out answers the unsigned question only. Signed overflow is V = Cn ⊕ Cn−1: same-signed operands producing the opposite sign.
  6. Subtraction is free. Four XOR gates and the carry in turn the adder into an adder-subtractor, because A − B is A + NOT B + 1.
Next in this courseCarry-lookahead and fast adders: computing every carry directly from the inputs with generate and propagate terms, so the delay stops growing with the width — the answer to §9's 97.5 ns.
keynotes: 1 + 1 = 10, so a one-bit addition needs a sum and a carry.
The half adder is S = A ⊕ B, C = A·B; the full adder is S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B), and is exactly two half adders with their carries ORed.
Ripple-carry costs (2n + 1) gate delays, signed overflow is V = Cn ⊕ C(n−1), and four XOR gates plus the carry in make subtraction free.
